record.original_question: Determine the chromatic number of the unit-distance graph of the Euclidean plane.

evidence.quote: Problem 10.1 Find the chromatic number of the unit distance graph.

artifact.self_contained_problem: Let $G$ be the graph whose vertex set is the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$, with two points $x,y \in \mathbb{R}^2$ joined by an edge if and only if their Euclidean distance $\|x-y\|$ equals $1$. The chromatic number $\chi(G)$ is the least cardinal $k$ for which there exists a function $c:\mathbb{R}^2 \to \{1,2,\dots,k\}$ such that $c(x)\neq c(y)$ whenever $\|x-y\|=1$. Determine $\chi(G)$.
artifact.status_search_result: This is the Hadwiger–Nelson problem, posed in 1950. Classical bounds give 4 ≤ χ ≤ 7. In 2018, Aubrey D.N.J. de Grey constructed a unit-distance graph requiring 5 colors, raising the lower bound to 5. The upper bound of 7 (from a hexagonal tiling coloring) remains the best known. The exact value is still unknown as of 2026.

status_evidence.title: The chromatic number of the plane is at least 5
status_evidence.snippet: We present a family of finite unit-distance graphs in the plane that are not 4-colourable...
status_evidence.claim: de Grey improved the lower bound to 5 in 2018; the upper bound of 7 remains, so the problem is open.

status_evidence.title: Hadwiger–Nelson problem
status_evidence.snippet: The answer is unknown, but has been narrowed down to one of the numbers 5, 6 or 7.
status_evidence.claim: The exact chromatic number of the plane is still unknown, with current bounds 5 ≤ χ ≤ 7.
